brief: The Market Ear argues US fiscal deficits have become the dominant market driver: in the first 11 months of fiscal 2026 the government collected $4.8tn but spent $6.8tn, a $2tn gap outside recession. Debt issued during the cheap-money era is refinancing at much higher rates with a lag, so net interest expense has already overtaken defense and Medicare as a share of GDP and is forecast to double from ~$1tn today to $2.1tn by 2035, near 5% of GDP. Developed-world deficits and debt-to-GDP ratios already exceed pre-GFC levels even in a healthy economy. The bond market has noticed: the 30-year Treasury yield posted its highest weekly close in over 22 years, and AI-capex demand is now competing with expanding sovereign issuance for the same private capital, raising its price. Since entitlements drive roughly 70% of spending and, with net interest, consume 98.4% of federal receipts, spending cuts alone cannot fix it. With little political appetite for spending cuts or tax hikes, the piece concludes the gap is more likely closed via inflation or higher interest rates.

cards.claim: In the first 11 months of fiscal 2026, the US government collected $4.8 trillion in revenue but spent $6.8 trillion, a roughly $2 trillion deficit outside of a recession.
cards.anchor: the US government collected $4.8 trillion — and spent $6.8 trillion

cards.claim: US net interest expense has overtaken both defense spending and Medicare as a share of GDP.
cards.anchor: US net interest expense has now overtaken both defense and Medicare as a share of GDP.

cards.claim: US net interest costs are forecast to roughly double from about $1 trillion currently to $2.1 trillion by 2035, near 5% of GDP.
cards.anchor: US net interest costs are expected to double from ~$1trn today to $2.1trn by 2035, nearly 5% of GDP.

cards.claim: Much of the US government's outstanding debt still carries low coupons from the cheap-money era and is being refinanced at today's much higher rates as it matures, so the fiscal pain from higher rates arrives with a lag.
cards.anchor: As that debt matures, it is steadily being refinanced at today's much higher rates.

cards.claim: Deficits across much of the developed world are already far larger than they were before the global financial crisis, even with the economy currently healthy.
cards.anchor: Deficits across much of the developed world are already far larger than they were before the GFC.

cards.claim: Government debt-to-GDP ratios across the developed world have surged, leaving governments more exposed to higher real interest rates.
cards.anchor:
Government debt-to-GDP ratios have surged —
leaving governments far more exposed to higher real rates.

cards.claim: The 30-year US Treasury yield posted its highest weekly close in more than 22 years.
cards.anchor:
The 30-year Treasury yield just posted its highest weekly
close in more than 22 years.

cards.claim: The AI capex boom, exploding sovereign debt issuance, and central banks stepping back as buyers are causing governments, hyperscalers and infrastructure investors to increasingly compete for the same private capital, raising its price.
cards.anchor:
Governments, hyperscalers and
infrastructure are increasingly competing for the same private capital.

cards.claim: Roughly 70% of US federal spending is driven by entitlement programs.
cards.anchor: Roughly 70% of US federal spending is driven by entitlements.

cards.claim: US net interest expense combined with Social Security, Medicare, healthcare and veterans' benefits now consumes 98.4% of federal government receipts, near a record high.
cards.anchor:
Net interest plus Social Security, Medicare, healthcare and veterans' benefits now consume 98.4% of
federal government receipts

cards.claim: Given limited political appetite for spending cuts or tax increases, the fiscal gap is more likely to eventually be closed through inflation or higher interest rates than through reduced spending or higher taxes.
cards.anchor: Something eventually has to give: spending, taxes, inflation or interest rates.
